summary.text: Using the absorption identity for binomial coefficients, the proof establishes integrality and splits the numerator difference at one Dwork step into terms with indices divisible by \(p\) and those not divisible by \(p\). Generalized Lucas lifting, Taylor expansions of shifted products and inverse squares, finite-field power-sum/Wolstenholme congruences, and an inductive divisibility bound for binomial moments show both parts are divisible by \(p^{4(v_p(m)+1)}\); dividing by \(pm\) yields the required \(p^{3(v_p(m)+1)}\) one-step congruence, which implies the stated modulus.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 a(N)=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N}(N+2k)\binom{N+k-1}{k}^{3}\qquad(N\geq1),
\]
and put
\[
 F(N)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}(N+2k)\binom{N+k-1}{k}^{3}.
\]
We prove a stronger one-step assertion and then iterate it in the required form.

Throughout, \(p\geq5\) is prime and \(v_p\) denotes the usual \(p\)-adic valuation. Statements about the valuation of rational numbers are interpreted in \(\mathbb Q_p\). Every denominator used below is prime to \(p\), so these statements can equivalently be read after clearing denominators as ordinary integer divisibility statements.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Integrality and elementary binomial identities
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We repeatedly use the absorption identity
\[
 k\binom{N+k-1}{k}=N\binom{N+k-1}{k-1}\qquad(N,k\geq1).
\tag{1}
\]
It follows directly from the factorial formula for the binomial coefficients. Consequently,
\[
 (N+2k)\binom{N+k-1}{k}^{3}
 =N\left(\binom{N+k-1}{k}^{3}
 +2\binom{N+k-1}{k-1}\binom{N+k-1}{k}^{2}\right)
\tag{2}
\]
for \(k\geq1\); the \(k=0\) term is also divisible by \(N\). Thus \(N\mid F(N)\), and
\[
 F(N)=N a(N).
\tag{3}
\]
This also proves directly that the displayed formula defining \(a(N)\) is integral.

A consequence of (1) that will be useful is this: if \(p^t\mid N\), \(k\geq1\), and \(p\nmid k\), then
\[
 p^t\mid \binom{N+k-1}{k}.
\tag{4}
\]
Indeed, (1) says that \(p^t\) divides \(k\binom{N+k-1}{k}\), and \(k\) is invertible modulo \(p^t\).

We will also use the upward form
\[
 m\binom{m+j}{j}=(m+j)\binom{m+j-1}{j}.
\tag{5}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. A generalized Lucas lifting
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We first prove the congruence
\[
 \binom{pA}{pB}\equiv\binom AB\pmod {p^t}
 \quad\text{if }B\leq A,\ t\geq1,\ p^{t-1}\mid A-B.
\tag{6}
\]
To see this without division by a possibly nonunit binomial coefficient, separate from the factorial products all factors divisible by \(p\). If
\[
 P=\prod_{\substack{1\leq i\leq pB\\p\nmid i}}i,
 \qquad
 Q=\prod_{\substack{1\leq i\leq pB\\p\nmid i}}\bigl(p(A-B)+i\bigr),
\]
then cancellation of the factors divisible by \(p\) in the factorial identity gives the exact integer equality
\[
 \binom{pA}{pB}P=\binom AB Q.
\tag{7}
\]
Since \(p^t\mid p(A-B)\), we have \(Q\equiv P\pmod {p^t}\). Also \(P\) is prime to \(p\), and hence is cancellable modulo \(p^t\). This proves (6).

We need a slightly shifted version. If \(p^t\mid X\), \(j\geq1\), and \(p\nmid j\), Pascal's identity together with
\[
 j\binom{X+j}{j}=(X+j)\binom{X+j-1}{j-1}
\]
gives
\[
 \binom{X+j}{j}\equiv\binom{X+j-1}{j-1}\pmod {p^t},
\tag{8}
\]
because \(X+j\equiv j\pmod {p^t}\) and \(j\) is invertible modulo \(p^t\). Repeating (8) through the last \(b\) positions, where \(0\leq b<p\), and then applying (6), gives the generalized Lucas lifting
\[
 \boxed{
 \binom{pM+pq+b}{pq+b}\equiv\binom{M+q}{q}\pmod {p^t}}
\tag{9}
\]
provided \(t\geq1\) and \(p^{t-1}\mid M\). Indeed, none of
\(pq+b,pq+b-1,\ldots,pq+1\) is divisible by \(p\), so (8) removes the final \(b\) positions; what remains is
\(\binom{p(M+q)}{pq}\), to which (6) applies.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Harmonic sums
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For \(h\geq1\) and \(n\geq1\), define
\[
 H_h(n)=\sum_{\substack{0\leq i<pn\\p\nmid i}}i^{-h}\in\mathbb Q_p.
\]
All summands are \(p\)-adic units.

We require
\[
 v_p(H_2(n))\geq e+1,
 \qquad
 v_p(H_1(n))\geq 2e+2
 \quad\text{whenever }p^e\mid n.
\tag{10}
\]
We prove these estimates.

First, in \(\mathbb F_p\),
\[
 \sum_{c=1}^{p-1}c^{-2}=0.
\tag{11}
\]
Indeed, \(c^{-2}=c^{p-3}\), and the sum of the \(d\)-th powers of all elements of \(\mathbb F_p\) is zero when \(0<d<p-1\). Splitting the integers below \(pn\) into blocks modulo \(p\), (11) gives
\(v_p(H_2(n))\geq1\), the case \(e=0\) of the first estimate.

For the induction step, suppose \(p^e\mid n'\). Every integer below \(p^2n'\) and prime to \(p\) is uniquely of the form
\[
 pn'a+c,
 \quad 0\leq a<p,
 \quad 0\leq c<pn',\quad p\nmid c.
\]
For \(c\) and \(c+x\) nonzero, the exact identity
\[
 (c+x)^{-2}-c^{-2}
 =-2x c^{-3}+(c+x)^{-2}c^{-3}x^2(3c+2x)
\tag{12}
\]
holds. Apply this with \(x=pn'a\) and sum. The constant terms give
\(pH_2(n')\), whose valuation is at least \(e+2\) by induction. The sum of the linear terms factors as
\[
 -pn'\left(2\sum_{a=0}^{p-1}a\right)H_3(n').

def\]
Here \(2\sum_{a=0}^{p-1}a=p(p-1)\), so this also has valuation at least \(e+2\). Finally, every remainder in (12) contains \(x^2\), hence has valuation at least \(2e+2\), which is at least \(e+2\). The ultrametric inequality therefore yields
\[
 v_p(H_2(pn'))\geq e+2.
\]
This proves the first part of (10) by induction.

For \(H_1\), reflect the indexing set by \(i\mapsto pn-i\). For nonzero \(a,b\), the exact identity
\[
 a^{-1}+b^{-1}
 =-(a+b)a^{-2}-(a+b)^2a^{-3}+(a+b)^3a^{-3}b^{-1}
\tag{13}
\]
holds. Taking \(a=i\), \(b=pn-i\), and summing gives
\[
 2H_1(n)=-pnH_2(n)-(pn)^2H_3(n)+(pn)^3W,
\tag{14}
\]
where
\[
 W=\sum_{\substack{0\leq i<pn\\p\nmid i}}i^{-3}(pn-i)^{-1}

def\]
has valuation at least zero. If \(p^e\mid n\), the three terms on the right of (14) have valuations at least, respectively,
\[
 (e+1)+(e+1)=2e+2,
 \quad 2e+2,
 \quad 3e+3.
\]
Since \(p\geq5\), 2 is a \(p\)-adic unit, proving the second estimate in (10).

We will also use the standard finite-field power sum consequence
\[
 v_p\left(\sum_{c=1}^{p-1}c^{-d}\right)\geq1
 \quad\text{if }(p-1)\nmid d.
\tag{15}
\]
This follows because inversion permutes \(\mathbb F_p^\times\), and the sum of the \(d\)-th powers of its elements vanishes unless \(p-1\mid d\). Without the hypothesis, the same sum still has valuation at least zero.

For completeness, the congruence often called Wolstenholme's harmonic congruence also follows from the same ingredients:
\[
 \sum_{c=1}^{p-1}c^{-1}\equiv0\pmod {p^2}.
\tag{16}
\]
Pair \(c\) with \(p-c\). Their inverse sum modulo \(p^2\) is
\(p(c(p-c))^{-1}\); reducing the remaining factor modulo \(p\) turns the total into \(-p\sum c^{-2}\), which vanishes by (11). This is consistent with (10) at \(n=1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. The master binomial sums
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For \(M\geq1\) and \(\ell\geq0\), put
\[
 T_\ell(M)=\sum_{q=0}^{M-1}\binom{M+q}{q}^{3}q^\ell.
\]
If \(p^s\mid M\), we claim
\[
 v_p(T_\ell(M))\geq \max(s-\ell,0),
\tag{17}
\]
and, when \(\ell\geq1\), the stronger estimate
\[
 v_p(T_\ell(M))\geq \max(s+1-\ell,0).
\tag{18}
\]

Here is the induction proving both assertions. The case \(s=0\) is immediate. For the step write \(M=pM'\), where \(p^{s-1}\mid M'\), and write every \(q<M\) uniquely as \(q=pq'+b\), with \(q'<M'\), \(0\leq b<p\). By (9),
\[
 \binom{pM'+pq'+b}{pq'+b}^{3}
 \equiv \binom{M'+q'}{q'}^{3}\pmod {p^s}.
\tag{19}
\]
Thus replacing the first cube by the second produces an error divisible by \(p^s\), which is sufficient for both claimed bounds at this induction level. For the main part expand
\[
 (pq'+b)^\ell=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell}\binom\ell i p^i(q')^i b^{\ell-i}.
\tag{20}
\]
After summing, the \(i\)-th term contains
\[
 p^i\left(\sum_{q'<M'}\binom{M'+q'}{q'}^3(q')^i\right)
 \left(\sum_{b=0}^{p-1}b^{\ell-i}\right).
\tag{21}
\]
The induction hypothesis supplies all required powers of \(p\) for (17). For (18), the same is true when \(i\geq1\), using the strengthened induction hypothesis. When \(i=0\) and \(\ell\geq2\), the unstrengthened bound (17) already suffices because the requested exponent has dropped by at least one. When \(i=0,\ell=1\), the missing power is supplied by
\[
 \sum_{b=0}^{p-1}b=\frac{p(p-1)}2,

def\]
which is divisible by \(p\) because \(p\) is odd. This completes the induction and proves (17) and (18).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. A generating inverse-square sum
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Suppose \(p^s\mid M\), and define
\[
 G=\sum_{q=0}^{M-1}\binom{M+q}{q}^{3}
       \sum_{c=1}^{p-1}(pq+c)^{-2}.
\]
We claim
\[
 v_p(G)\geq s+1.
\tag{22}
\]

Use the finite Taylor expansion
\[
 (c+A)^{-2}
 =\sum_{\ell=0}^{s}(\ell+1)(-1)^\ell A^\ell c^{-\ell-2}+R_{s}(A,c),
\tag{23}
\]
where the exact remainder is
\[
 R_s(A,c)=(-A)^{s+1}\bigl((s+2)c+(s+1)A\bigr)c^{-s-2}(c+A)^{-2}.
\tag{24}
\]
This identity follows after multiplying by \((c+A)^2c^{s+2}\) and summing the resulting finite geometric derivative; thus no convergence issue is involved. Put \(A=pq\). Every factor in (24) except \(A^{s+1}\) is \(p\)-integral, so the total contribution of the remainders has valuation at least \(s+1\).

For the \(\ell\)-th main term, after summing first over \(q\) and \(c\), the relevant product is, up to \(p\)-integral scalar factors,
\[
 p^\ell T_\ell(M)W_{\ell+2},
 \qquad W_d=\sum_{c=1}^{p-1}c^{-d}.
\tag{25}
\]
If \((p-1)\nmid \ell+2\), (15), together with (17), gives valuation at least
\[
 \ell+\max(s-\ell,0)+1\geq s+1

def\]
(for \(\ell\leq s\), as in (23)). If \((p-1)\mid\ell+2\), then \(\ell\neq0\), because \(p-1\geq4\); hence (18) applies and gives
\[
 \ell+\max(s+1-\ell,0)\geq s+1.

def\]
Thus every term in (23), and its remainder, has the required valuation, proving (22).

The generalized Lucas congruence (9), with \(b=c-1\), gives
\[
 \binom{pM+pq+c-1}{pq+c-1}
 \equiv \binom{M+q}{q}\pmod {p^{s+1}}.
\tag{26}
\]
A difference of cubes is divisible by the difference of their bases, so replacing the cube in (22) by
\(\binom{pM+pq+c-1}{pq+c-1}^{3}\) changes the sum by something of valuation at least \(s+1\). Therefore
\[
 \boxed{
 v_p\left(
 \sum_{q=0}^{M-1}\sum_{c=1}^{p-1}
 \binom{pM+pq+c-1}{pq+c-1}^{3}(pq+c)^{-2}
 \right)\geq s+1.}
\tag{27}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. The nonaligned contribution
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Set \(N=pM\), with \(p^s\mid M\). The terms with \(p\nmid k\), where \(1\leq k\leq pM\), are parameterized uniquely as
\(k=pq+c\), \(0\leq q<M\), \(1\leq c<p\). Let
\[
 C_k=\binom{pM+k-1}{k},\qquad D_k=\binom{pM+k-1}{k-1}.
\]
By (1), \(kC_k=pM D_k\). Consequently the exact identity
\[
 (pM+2k)C_k^3
 =pM C_k^3+2(pM)^3D_k^3k^{-2}
\tag{28}
\]
holds in \(\mathbb Q_p\).

For the first term on the right, (4) says that \(v_p(C_k)\geq s+1\), while \(v_p(pM)\geq s+1\). Hence each such term has valuation at least \(4s+4\). For the sum of the second terms, factor out \(2(pM)^3\), of valuation at least \(3s+3\), and apply (27) to the remaining double sum. Its valuation is at least \(s+1\). We have proved
\[
 v_p\left(
 \sum_{\substack{0\leq k\leq pM\\p\nmid k}}
 (pM+2k)\binom{pM+k-1}{k}^{3}
 \right)\geq4s+4.
\tag{29}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. The aligned contribution
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We now treat \(k=pj\), \(0\leq j\leq M\). For \(j\geq1\), write
\[
 C_1=\binom{p(m+j)-1}{pj},\qquad C_0=\binom{m+j-1}{j},

def\]
where eventually \(m=M\). Separating from the factorial products the factors divisible by \(p\), exactly as in (7), gives
\[
 C_1=C_0R,
 \qquad
 R=\prod_{\substack{1\leq i\leq pj\\p\nmid i}}
 \left(1+\frac{pm}{i}\right).
\tag{30}
\]
This is an equality in \(\mathbb Q_p\). It can also be obtained by combining (5) with the unshifted product identity (7).

Let
\[
 s=v_p(m),\qquad e=v_p(j),\qquad \alpha=\min(s,e).
\]
Then \(p^\alpha\mid m+j\) and \(p^\alpha\mid m+2j\). Moreover,
\[
 v_p(C_0)\geq s-\alpha.
\tag{31}
\]
If \(s\leq e\), this is trivial. If \(e<s\), write \(j=p^e j_0\) with \(p\nmid j_0\). From (1),
\(p^s\mid jC_0\); canceling \(p^e j_0\) gives \(p^{s-e}\mid C_0\), proving (31).

We next establish
\[
 v_p(R^3-1)\geq s+2\alpha+3.
\tag{32}
\]
Reflect the factors in (30) by \(i\mapsto pj-i\), a permutation of the integers in the product. Multiplying the original and reflected products gives
\[
 R^2=\prod_{\substack{1\leq i\leq pj\\p\nmid i}}(1+z_i),
 \qquad
 z_i=\frac{p^2m(m+j)}{i(pj-i)}.
\tag{33}
\]
Both denominator factors are prime to \(p\), so
\[
 v_p(z_i)\geq s+\alpha+2.
\tag{34}
\]
For any finite collection of \(p\)-adically small \(z_i\),
\[
 \prod_i(1+z_i)-1-\sum_i z_i

def\]
has valuation at least twice the minimum valuation of the \(z_i\), since every term left after removing the constant and linear terms contains at least two of them.

It remains to estimate the linear sum. The partial-fraction identity
\[
 \frac1{i(pj-i)}=\frac1{pj}\left(\frac1i+\frac1{pj-i}\right)

def\]
and reflection yield
\[
 \sum_i z_i
 =2pm(m+j)j^{-1}H_1(j),
\tag{35}
\]
where the sum defining \(H_1(j)\) runs over the same nonmultiples of \(p\) below \(pj\). By (10),
\(v_p(H_1(j))\geq2e+2\), while \(v_p(j^{-1})=-e\). Thus the right side of (35) has valuation at least
\[
 1+s+\alpha-e+(2e+2)=s+\alpha+e+3\geq s+2\alpha+3.

def\]
The quadratic remainder following (34) has valuation at least
\(2s+2\alpha+4\geq s+2\alpha+3\). Therefore
\[
 v_p(R^2-1)\geq s+2\alpha+3.
\tag{36}
\]
Also (30) immediately gives \(v_p(R-1)\geq s+1>0\). Since \(p\geq5\), both 2 and 3 are units, and if \(R\equiv1\pmod p\), then
\[
 v_p(R^3-1)=v_p(R-1)=v_p(R^2-1);

def\]
indeed \(R+1\) and \(R^2+R+1\) are units. This proves (32).

Now the aligned summand in the difference \(F(pm)-pF(m)\) is
\[
 p(m+2j)(C_1^3-C_0^3)
 =p(m+2j)C_0^3(R^3-1).
\]
Using \(v_p(m+2j)\geq\alpha\), (31), and (32), its valuation is at least
\[
 1+\alpha+3(s-\alpha)+(s+2\alpha+3)=4s+4.
\tag{37}
\]
For \(j=0\), the difference of the two binomial cubes is zero. Hence the entire aligned contribution has valuation at least \(4s+4\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
8. The numerator congruence
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Split the defining sum for \(F(pM)\) according as \(p\mid k\) or not. For \(k=pj\), subtract the corresponding term of \(pF(M)\). This gives the exact identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
F(pM)-pF(M)
={}&\sum_{j=0}^{M}p(M+2j)
 \left[
 \binom{p(M+j)-1}{pj}^{3}-\binom{M+j-1}{j}^{3}
 \right]\\
&+\sum_{q=0}^{M-1}\sum_{c=1}^{p-1}
 \bigl(pM+2(pq+c)\bigr)
 \binom{pM+pq+c-1}{pq+c}^{3}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{38}
\]
If \(s=v_p(M)\), the first line has valuation at least \(4s+4\) by (37), and the second has valuation at least \(4s+4\) by (29). Thus
\[
 \boxed{p^{4s+4}\mid F(pM)-pF(M).}
\tag{39}
\]
Although derived using \(p\)-adic notation, the quantity in (39) is an integer, so the valuation statement is exactly the displayed ordinary divisibility.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
9. Passage from the numerator to \(a(N)\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Write \(M=p^su\), where \(p\nmid u\). By (3),
\[
\begin{aligned}
F(pM)-pF(M)
 &=pM\,a(pM)-pM\,a(M)\\
 &=p^{s+1}u\bigl(a(pM)-a(M)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
	ag{40}
\]
Combining (39) and (40), cancel \(p^{s+1}\); then cancel \(u\), which is prime to \(p\). We obtain the stronger one-step congruence
\[
 \boxed{a(pM)\equiv a(M)\pmod {p^{3(s+1)}}},
 \qquad s=v_p(M).
\tag{41}
\]

Finally, let \(n,r\) be positive and put
\[
 M=np^{r-1}.

def\]
Then \(pM=np^r\), and
\[
 v_p(M)=v_p(n)+r-1\geq r-1.

def\]
Applying (41) gives
\[
 a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})
 \pmod {p^{3(v_p(M)+1)}}.

def\]
Since \(3(v_p(M)+1)\geq3r\), this congruence remains true modulo \(p^{3r}\). Therefore, for every prime \(p\geq5\) and all positive integers \(n,r\),
\[
 \boxed{a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r}}}.
\]
This is the desired supercongruence.
